items.stem: Which of the following best describes "conservation of charge"?
options: A long coil of wire which, when carrying a current, produces a nearly uniform magnetic field inside it
A surface on which all points have the same electric potential
The total electric charge of an isolated system remains constant
The electric force per unit positive charge on a small test charge placed at a point, E = F/q
items.answer: The total electric charge of an isolated system remains constant
items.markingKey: C. "conservation of charge" is the total electric charge of an isolated system remains constant.

items.stem: Distinguish between Newton's law of gravitation and Coulomb's law.
items.answer: Both are inverse-square laws for point sources; electric forces can attract or repel and depend on charge with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², while gravity only attracts, depends on mass and G is about 10²⁰ times smaller.
items.markingKey: Both are inverse-square laws for point sources; electric forces can attract or repel and depend on charge with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², while gravity only attracts, depends on mass and G is about 10²⁰ times smaller. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which of the following statements about electric charge, Coulomb's law and conservation of charge is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Arjun.)
options: A positively charged object has gained protons.
Zero field means zero potential gradient, not zero potential: e.g. inside a charged conducting sphere E = 0 but V = kQ/R.
Magnetic field lines form closed loops: outside a magnet they go N to S, inside S to N; there are no magnetic monopoles.
Field lines show the force on a positive charge; an electron is pushed in the opposite direction.
items.answer: A positively charged object has gained protons.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: It has lost electrons; protons are bound in nuclei and do not move in everyday charging.

items.stem: A student claims: "Rubbing a rod creates charge on it." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Charge is transferred, not created: the cloth gains an equal and opposite charge (conservation of charge).
items.markingKey: Charge is transferred, not created: the cloth gains an equal and opposite charge (conservation of charge). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Noah investigated Coulomb’s law using a charged pith ball on a thread and measured its deflection. The 5 readings of the deflection angle of a charged pith ball near a charged sphere were 11.0, 10.9, 11.1, 11.2, 11.3 °. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures.
items.markingKey: Mean = 11.1 ° (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.2 ° (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.2/11.1 × 100 = 1.8 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty.

items.stem: Two identical small balls, each of mass 0.20 g, hang from a common point on insulating threads 0.50 m long. They are given equal charges and come to rest with each thread at 10° to the vertical. (a) Draw a free-body diagram for one ball. (b) Determine the electric force on each ball. (c) Determine the charge on each ball.
items.answer: (a) weight down, tension along the thread, electric force horizontal away from the other ball; (b) F = mg tan 10° = 3.46 × 10⁻⁴ N; (c) separation = 2 × 0.50 sin 10° = 0.174 m; q = r√(F/k) = 3.4 × 10⁻⁸ C.
items.markingKey: Three forces correctly shown (A1); T cos θ = mg and T sin θ = F (M1); F = 3.46 × 10⁻⁴ N (A1); separation 0.174 m (A1); q = 3.4 × 10⁻⁸ C (A1).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "elementary charge".
items.answer: The magnitude of the charge on a proton or electron, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; all free charges are whole-number multiples of it
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the magnitude of the charge on a proton or electron, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; all free charges are whole-number multiples of it. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of these charges could NOT exist on an isolated object?
items.markingKey: A. 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ C = 1.5e is not a whole multiple of e.

items.stem: Explain why electric forces dominate over gravitational forces between an electron and a proton.
items.answer: The ratio F_e/F_g = ke²/(Gmₑmₚ) ≈ 2 × 10³⁹ because k is enormous compared with G and the masses are tiny; gravity only dominates for large neutral bodies.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The ratio F_e/F_g = ke²/(Gmₑmₚ) ≈ 2 × 10³⁹ because k is enormous compared with G and the masses are tiny; gravity only dominates for large neutral bodies. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Tariq writes: "Rubbing a rod creates charge on it." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Charge is transferred, not created: the cloth gains an equal and opposite charge (conservation of charge).
items.markingKey: Charge is transferred, not created: the cloth gains an equal and opposite charge (conservation of charge). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Two point charges exert a force of 24 N on each other. One charge is multiplied by 1 and the separation is multiplied by 3. What is the new force?
A small sphere carries a charge of −1.60 × 10⁻¹⁷ C. How many excess electrons are on it?
A dust particle has a charge of 4.80 × 10⁻⁹ C. Determine the number of electrons it has lost.
items.answer: 3.00 × 10¹⁰ electrons

items.stem: "The inverse-square form of Coulomb’s law is exact." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: It is one of the most precisely tested laws in physics, accurate to extraordinary precision in its domain; "exact" is a claim science can only support to a measured limit.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: experiments limit deviations of the exponent from 2 to less than 10⁻¹⁶; it follows from field lines spreading over 4πr². Arguments against: at sub-atomic distances quantum effects modify the interaction; in materials ε differs from ε₀; all laws are tested to finite precision (NOS). Supported judgement: It is one of the most precisely tested laws in physics, accurate to extraordinary precision in its domain; "exact" is a claim science can only support to a measured limit. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The electric force per unit positive charge on a small test charge placed at a point, E = F/q"?
items.answer: electric field strength
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of electric field strength.

items.stem: Which field pattern has straight, parallel, equally spaced lines?
options: between two oppositely charged parallel plates
items.answer: between two oppositely charged parallel plates
items.markingKey: C. Uniform field.

items.stem: "Doubling the plate separation at constant voltage doubles the field strength." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: E = V/d, so doubling d halves E.
items.markingKey: E = V/d, so doubling d halves E. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Parallel plates 10 mm apart have a p.d. of 300 V. What is the electric field strength between them?
Two positive point charges, +2.0 nC and +8.0 nC, are 30 cm apart. Find the position between them where the electric field strength is zero.
items.answer: 10.0 cm from the +2.0 nC charge

items.stem: In a Millikan-type experiment an oil drop of mass 2.40 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held stationary between horizontal plates 5.0 mm apart. The drop carries 5 excess electrons. Calculate the field strength and the potential difference required.

An inkjet printer uses charged droplets deflected by a uniform electric field. Discuss how the deflection of a droplet depends on its charge, mass, speed and the field, and suggest why the printer charges droplets by different amounts.
items.answer: In the plates the droplet has acceleration a = qE/m perpendicular to its velocity; time between plates t = L/v; deflection y = ½(qE/m)(L/v)². So y ∝ q, ∝ E, ∝ 1/m and ∝ 1/v². By giving each droplet a different charge, the printer places drops at different positions on the paper with fixed plates.
items.markingKey: a = qE/m (M1); t = L/v (M1); y = qEL²/(2mv²) (A1); dependence on each variable stated (R1); charge controls landing position (R1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The concept of a field is merely a calculation tool rather than a physical reality."
items.answer: Fields began as a model (Faraday), but the propagation of electromagnetic waves carrying energy shows they are physical entities.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: forces can be computed by Coulomb’s law without mentioning fields. Arguments against: fields carry energy and momentum (e.g. electromagnetic waves); changes propagate at finite speed c; field theories underpin modern physics. Supported judgement: Fields began as a model (Faraday), but the propagation of electromagnetic waves carrying energy shows they are physical entities. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Electric field lines start on
options: negative charges and end on positive charges
positive charges and end on negative charges
items.answer: positive charges and end on negative charges
items.markingKey: C. Direction of force on a positive test charge.

items.stem: Define the term "electric field strength".
items.answer: The electric force per unit positive charge on a small test charge placed at a point, E = F/q
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the electric force per unit positive charge on a small test charge placed at a point, E = F/q. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the field between two large parallel plates is uniform except near the edges.
items.answer: Between the plates the field lines run straight from one plate to the other, parallel and equally spaced, so E = V/d everywhere; at the edges the lines bulge outwards (fringing) and the field weakens.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Between the plates the field lines run straight from one plate to the other, parallel and equally spaced, so E = V/d everywhere; at the edges the lines bulge outwards (fringing) and the field weakens. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Nia writes four statements while revising electric field strength and field patterns; uniform fields between plates. Which one is a misconception?
options: It has lost electrons; protons are bound in nuclei and do not move in everyday charging.
V = kQ/r falls as 1/r; E = kQ/r² falls as 1/r².
Zero field means zero potential gradient, not zero potential: e.g. inside a charged conducting sphere E = 0 but V = kQ/R.
Doubling the plate separation at constant voltage doubles the field strength.
items.answer: Doubling the plate separation at constant voltage doubles the field strength.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: E = V/d, so doubling d halves E.

items.stem: Parallel plates 5 mm apart have a p.d. of 600 V. What is the electric field strength between them?
A student claims: "An electron in an electric field is pushed along the direction of the field lines." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Field lines show the force on a positive charge; an electron is pushed in the opposite direction.
items.markingKey: Field lines show the force on a positive charge; an electron is pushed in the opposite direction. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Parallel plates 4 mm apart have a p.d. of 500 V. What is the electric field strength between them?
Point charges of +2.0 nC and −8.0 nC are 20 cm apart. Determine the magnitude and direction of the electric field at the midpoint.
items.answer: 8990 N C⁻¹ directed away from the +2.0 nC charge

items.stem: In a Millikan-type experiment, plates are 6.0 mm apart. A drop of mass 2.9 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held stationary when the p.d. is 355 V. (a) Determine the charge on the drop. (b) How many electrons does it carry? (c) The p.d. is increased to 500 V; calculate the initial acceleration of the drop and its direction.
"A Faraday cage gives complete protection from all electric fields and radiation." Discuss.
items.answer: It shields static fields and long-wavelength radiation effectively, but not all fields, so "complete" is an overstatement.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: static fields inside a closed conductor are zero; cars protect occupants from lightning. Arguments against: holes allow radiation of wavelength smaller than the mesh to enter; magnetic fields at low frequency are not blocked; contact with the cage can still be dangerous. Supported judgement: It shields static fields and long-wavelength radiation effectively, but not all fields, so "complete" is an overstatement. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "magnetic field"?
options: The electric force per unit positive charge on a small test charge placed at a point, E = F/q
The strength of a magnetic field, measured in tesla (T); 1 T is the field in which a 1 m wire carrying 1 A at right angles experiences a force of 1 N
A field of constant magnitude and direction, as between parallel charged plates, where E = V/d
A region in which a moving charge, a current-carrying conductor or a magnet experiences a force
items.answer: A region in which a moving charge, a current-carrying conductor or a magnet experiences a force
items.markingKey: D. "magnetic field" is a region in which a moving charge, a current-carrying conductor or a magnet experiences a force.

items.stem: A student wants to test the relationship B = μ₀I/(2πr) for the field of a long straight wire measured with a Hall probe at different distances r. State which quantities should be plotted on the axes to obtain a straight-line graph, and state what the gradient represents.
items.answer: Plot B (y-axis) against 1/r (x-axis); gradient = μ₀I/2π, from which μ₀ can be found. A straight line through the origin confirms B ∝ 1/r.
items.markingKey: Correct choice of axes: B against 1/r (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = μ₀I/2π, from which μ₀ can be found (A1). A straight line through the origin confirms B ∝ 1/r.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the field inside a long solenoid and the field of a long straight wire.
items.answer: Around a wire, the lines are concentric circles and B = μ₀I/(2πr) decreases with distance; inside a solenoid, the lines are parallel to the axis and B = μ₀nI is uniform, independent of position.
items.markingKey: Around a wire, the lines are concentric circles and B = μ₀I/(2πr) decreases with distance; inside a solenoid, the lines are parallel to the axis and B = μ₀nI is uniform, independent of position. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Magnetic field lines start on the north pole and end on the south pole, like electric field lines." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Magnetic field lines form closed loops: outside a magnet they go N to S, inside S to N; there are no magnetic monopoles.
items.markingKey: Magnetic field lines form closed loops: outside a magnet they go N to S, inside S to N; there are no magnetic monopoles. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The field 2.0 cm from a long wire is 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ T. What current flows in the wire?
items.markingKey: B. I = 2πrB/μ₀ = 20.0 A.

A Hall probe measures the magnetic flux density B at distances r from a long straight wire carrying 4.0 A. Theory: B = μ₀I/(2πr).

r / cm | B / μT
1.0 | 78.9
1.5 | 53.2
2.0 | 39.8
3.0 | 26.7

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the permeability of free space μ₀. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State μ₀ with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) B in T (y) against 1/r in m⁻¹ (x); (b) gradient ≈ 7.89 × 10⁻⁷ T m; (c) 1.24 × 10⁻⁶ T m A⁻¹; (d) 1.24 × 10⁻⁶ T m A⁻¹ ± 5 × 10⁻⁸ T m A⁻¹

(c) μ₀ = 2π × gradient/I = 1.24 × 10⁻⁶ T m A⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 4 % of the value = 5 × 10⁻⁸ T m A⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.markingKey: D. B = μ₀I/(2πr).

items.stem: A student in Nairobi is checking notes on magnetic fields of wires, coils and solenoids. Which statement is incorrect?
options: Field lines show the direction of the force (and acceleration), not the trajectory; a moving particle can cross field lines.
A longer solenoid with the same turns and current has a stronger field.
V = kQ/r falls as 1/r; E = kQ/r² falls as 1/r².
Magnetic field lines form closed loops: outside a magnet they go N to S, inside S to N; there are no magnetic monopoles.
items.answer: A longer solenoid with the same turns and current has a stronger field.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: B = μ₀NI/L: spreading the same turns over a longer length reduces n and so reduces B.

items.stem: The number of turns per metre of a solenoid is doubled and the current halved. The field inside
items.answer: is unchanged
items.markingKey: C. B = μ₀nI.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Earth’s field must be considered when measuring the field of a wire with a compass.
items.answer: A compass aligns with the resultant of Earth’s horizontal field and the wire’s field, so the deflection depends on both.

items.answer: Partly serendipitous, but significant because Ørsted was looking for such a link and recognised its importance.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "equipotential surface".
items.answer: A surface on which all points have the same electric potential
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a surface on which all points have the same electric potential. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why the electric potential is a scalar while the field is a vector, and why this makes potentials easier to combine.
items.answer: Potential is work per unit charge (energy), which has no direction; potentials from several charges add algebraically, whereas fields must be added as vectors.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Potential is work per unit charge (energy), which has no direction; potentials from several charges add algebraically, whereas fields must be added as vectors. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sofia and a classmate in Dubai disagree about electric potential and potential energy (HL). Which statement is correct?
options: Rubbing a rod creates charge on it.
A longer solenoid with the same turns and current has a stronger field.
Doubling the plate separation at constant voltage doubles the field strength.
V = kQ/r falls as 1/r; E = kQ/r² falls as 1/r².
items.answer: V = kQ/r falls as 1/r; E = kQ/r² falls as 1/r².
items.markingKey: D. The other options are common misconceptions. V = kQ/r falls as 1/r; E = kQ/r² falls as 1/r².

items.stem: What is the electric potential at 20 cm from a +2.0 nC point charge?
items.markingKey: C. V = kQ/r = 89.9 V.

items.stem: A proton is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 1200 V. Calculate the energy gained in eV and in J, and its final speed.

Compare and contrast the gravitational potential around Earth with the electric potential around an isolated positive point charge, referring to formulae, sign, the shape of equipotentials and the work done in moving a test object to infinity.
items.answer: Both: potential ∝ 1/r with zero at infinity, spherical equipotentials, field = −potential gradient. Gravitational V = −GM/r is negative everywhere (attractive), work must be done ON a mass to take it to infinity. Electric V = +kQ/r is positive for a positive source; a positive test charge is repelled, so the field does work on it as it moves to infinity (energy released).
items.markingKey: Correct formulae (A1); 1/r dependence and spherical equipotentials common (R1); sign difference linked to attraction/repulsion (R1); work to infinity compared (R1); field as negative gradient in both (A1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 1 V, 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J"?
items.answer: electronvolt
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of electronvolt.

items.stem: Explain the difference between electric potential energy and electric potential.
items.answer: Potential (V = J C⁻¹) is a property of a point, V = kQ/r; potential energy (J) belongs to a charge placed there, Eₚ = qV.
items.markingKey: Potential (V = J C⁻¹) is a property of a point, V = kQ/r; potential energy (J) belongs to a charge placed there, Eₚ = qV. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.markingKey: Zero field means zero potential gradient, not zero potential: e.g. inside a charged conducting sphere E = 0 but V = kQ/R. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Gravitational and electric fields are fundamentally the same."
items.answer: They share mathematical structure but differ in sign behaviour, strength and underlying theory, so "the same" overstates the analogy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: both inverse-square fields with similar potential formulae; field and potential concepts apply identically. Arguments against: gravity is only attractive; electric forces attract and repel; there is no gravitational shielding; magnitudes differ by ~10³⁶; gravity is described by general relativity, electric fields by electromagnetism. Supported judgement: They share mathematical structure but differ in sign behaviour, strength and underlying theory, so "the same" overstates the analogy. items.stem: Two point charges, +3.0 nC at x = 0 and −3.0 nC at x = 0.40 m, lie on the x-axis. (a) Calculate the electric potential at x = 0.10 m and at x = 0.20 m. (b) Calculate the work done by an external agent moving a +1.0 nC charge from x = 0.10 m to x = 0.20 m. (c) Explain why the field at x = 0.20 m is not zero although the potential is.
items.answer: (a) at 0.10 m: V = k(3.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.10 − 3.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.30) = 180 V; at 0.20 m: 0 V; (b) W = qΔV = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ × (0 − 180) = −1.8 × 10⁻⁷ J (the field does positive work); (c) the field is the negative potential gradient; potentials cancel at the midpoint but the potential is still decreasing there, so E points from + to −.
items.markingKey: (a) at 0.10 m: V = k(3.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.10 − 3.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.30) = 180 V; at 0.20 m: 0 V; (b) W = qΔV = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ × (0 − 180) = −1.8 × 10⁻⁷ J (the field does positive work); (c) the field is the negative potential gradient; potentials cancel at the midpoint but the potential is still decreasing there, so E points from + to −.

items.markingKey: C. The other options are common misconceptions. V = kQ/r falls as 1/r; E = kQ/r² falls as 1/r².

items.stem: Distinguish between a radial field and a uniform field.
items.answer: A radial field around a point charge has E = kQ/r², decreasing with distance and lines spreading out; a uniform field between parallel plates has E = V/d, the same everywhere, with parallel equally spaced lines.
items.markingKey: A radial field around a point charge has E = kQ/r², decreasing with distance and lines spreading out; a uniform field between parallel plates has E = V/d, the same everywhere, with parallel equally spaced lines. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student in Hanoi is checking notes on electric charge, Coulomb's law and conservation of charge. Which statement is incorrect?
options: Field lines show the direction of the force (and acceleration), not the trajectory; a moving particle can cross field lines.
B = μ₀NI/L: spreading the same turns over a longer length reduces n and so reduces B.
Coulomb’s law applies to any two charged objects at any separation.
It has lost electrons; protons are bound in nuclei and do not move in everyday charging.
items.answer: Coulomb’s law applies to any two charged objects at any separation.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: It applies to point charges (or spherically symmetric charge distributions) in a vacuum; for other shapes the force must be summed over the distribution.

items.stem: Maya and a classmate in Kuala Lumpur disagree about magnetic fields of wires, coils and solenoids. Which statement is correct?
options: B = μ₀NI/L: spreading the same turns over a longer length reduces n and so reduces B.
Field lines show the path a charged particle will follow.
A longer solenoid with the same turns and current has a stronger field.
Doubling the plate separation at constant voltage doubles the field strength.
items.answer: B = μ₀NI/L: spreading the same turns over a longer length reduces n and so reduces B.
items.markingKey: A. The other options are common misconceptions. B = μ₀NI/L: spreading the same turns over a longer length reduces n and so reduces B.

items.stem: At the midpoint between charges +Q and −Q, which is correct?
options: neither is zero, and both are maximal
the field is zero but the potential is not
the potential is zero but the field is not
items.answer: the potential is zero but the field is not
items.markingKey: C. Potentials cancel (scalars); fields add (both point to −Q).

items.stem: A student in Bogotá is checking notes on electric field strength and field patterns; uniform fields between plates. Which statement is incorrect?
options: Doubling the plate separation at constant voltage doubles the field strength.
Zero field means zero potential gradient, not zero potential: e.g. inside a charged conducting sphere E = 0 but V = kQ/R.
It applies to point charges (or spherically symmetric charge distributions) in a vacuum; for other shapes the force must be summed over the distribution.
Magnetic field lines form closed loops: outside a magnet they go N to S, inside S to N; there are no magnetic monopoles.
items.answer: Doubling the plate separation at constant voltage doubles the field strength.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: E = V/d, so doubling d halves E.

items.stem: Three point charges lie on a straight line: A (+2.0 μC), then C (+2.0 μC) 20 cm to the right of A, then B (−3.0 μC) 15 cm to the right of C. Determine the resultant force on C.
items.answer: 3.30 N to the right
items.markingKey: Force from A: 0.899 N to the right (A1); force from B: 2.40 N to the right (A1); vector sum (M1) = 3.30 N to the right (A1).

items.stem: A long straight wire carries a current of 20 A. Calculate the magnetic flux density 1.0 cm from the wire. (B = μ₀I/2πr)
What is the electric potential at 10 cm from a +2.0 nC point charge?
items.markingKey: C. V = kQ/r = 180 V.

items.stem: Noah writes: "An electron in an electric field is pushed along the direction of the field lines." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Field lines show the force on a positive charge; an electron is pushed in the opposite direction.
items.markingKey: Field lines show the force on a positive charge; an electron is pushed in the opposite direction. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Mei used a light conducting ball on an insulating thread and a protractor scale to estimate electric forces. The 5 readings of the deflection angle of a charged pith ball near a charged sphere were 9.7, 10.0, 9.9, 9.9, 9.7 °. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures.
items.markingKey: Mean = 9.8 ° (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.2 ° (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.2/9.8 × 100 = 1.5 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty.

items.stem: A solenoid 25 cm long has 500 turns and carries 1 A. What is the field inside?
A particle of charge +e is accelerated from rest through 250 V. What kinetic energy does it gain?
Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The concept of a field is merely a calculation tool rather than a physical reality."
items.answer: Fields began as a model (Faraday), but the propagation of electromagnetic waves carrying energy shows they are physical entities.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: forces can be computed by Coulomb’s law without mentioning fields. Arguments against: fields carry energy and momentum (e.g. electromagnetic waves); changes propagate at finite speed c; field theories underpin modern physics. Supported judgement: Fields began as a model (Faraday), but the propagation of electromagnetic waves carrying energy shows they are physical entities.

items.stem: Point charges +4.0 μC at A and −2.0 μC at B are 0.30 m apart. (a) Calculate the force between them. (b) Find the point on the line AB (outside the segment) where a third charge would feel no resultant force. (c) Explain why no such point exists between A and B.
items.answer: (a) F = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁶/0.09 = 0.80 N, attractive; (b) beyond B: 4/(0.30 + x)² = 2/x² → x = 0.72 m beyond B; (c) between the charges the forces from +4 μC and −2 μC on a test charge point in the same direction, so they cannot cancel.
items.markingKey: (a) F = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁶/0.09 = 0.80 N, attractive; (b) beyond B: 4/(0.30 + x)² = 2/x² → x = 0.72 m beyond B; (c) between the charges the forces from +4 μC and −2 μC on a test charge point in the same direction, so they cannot cancel.

items.stem: "Ørsted’s discovery that a current deflects a compass was a lucky accident." Discuss.
items.answer: Partly serendipitous, but significant because Ørsted was looking for such a link and recognised its importance.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it was reportedly observed during a lecture demonstration. Arguments against: Ørsted had been searching for a link between electricity and magnetism, guided by natural philosophy; "chance favours the prepared mind" – serendipity requires recognising significance (NOS). Supported judgement: Partly serendipitous, but significant because Ørsted was looking for such a link and recognised its importance. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: "Gravitational and electric fields are fundamentally the same." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: They share mathematical structure but differ in sign behaviour, strength and underlying theory, so "the same" overstates the analogy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: both inverse-square fields with similar potential formulae; field and potential concepts apply identically. Arguments against: gravity is only attractive; electric forces attract and repel; there is no gravitational shielding; magnitudes differ by ~10³⁶; gravity is described by general relativity, electric fields by electromagnetism. Supported judgement: They share mathematical structure but differ in sign behaviour, strength and underlying theory, so "the same" overstates the analogy. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "electric field line"?
options: A line showing the direction of the force on a small positive test charge
The strength of a magnetic field, measured in tesla (T); 1 T is the field in which a 1 m wire carrying 1 A at right angles experiences a force of 1 N
The magnitude of the charge on a proton or electron, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; all free charges are whole-number multiples of it
The total electric charge of an isolated system remains constant
items.answer: A line showing the direction of the force on a small positive test charge
items.markingKey: A. "electric field line" is a line showing the direction of the force on a small positive test charge.

items.stem: The value of the Coulomb constant k is
items.answer: 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A long coil of wire which, when carrying a current, produces a nearly uniform magnetic field inside it"?
items.answer: solenoid
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of solenoid.

items.stem: Aiko writes: "Where the electric field is zero the potential must also be zero." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Zero field means zero potential gradient, not zero potential: e.g. inside a charged conducting sphere E = 0 but V = kQ/R.
items.markingKey: Zero field means zero potential gradient, not zero potential: e.g. inside a charged conducting sphere E = 0 but V = kQ/R. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between electric field strength and electric force.
items.answer: Field strength (N C⁻¹) is a property of the point, independent of the test charge; force (N) is the field multiplied by the charge placed there, F = qE.
items.markingKey: Field strength (N C⁻¹) is a property of the point, independent of the test charge; force (N) is the field multiplied by the charge placed there, F = qE. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between Coulomb's law and Newton's law of gravitation.
items.answer: Both are inverse-square laws for point sources; electric forces can attract or repel and depend on charge with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², while gravity only attracts, depends on mass and G is about 10²⁰ times smaller.
items.markingKey: Both are inverse-square laws for point sources; electric forces can attract or repel and depend on charge with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², while gravity only attracts, depends on mass and G is about 10²⁰ times smaller. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why magnetic field lines never cross.
items.answer: The field at any point has a single direction; if two lines crossed, the field would have two directions there.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The field at any point has a single direction; if two lines crossed, the field would have two directions there. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the electric potential energy of two like charges increases as they are pushed together.
items.answer: Work must be done against the repulsive force to bring them closer; this work is stored as electric potential energy, Eₚ = kq₁q₂/r, which increases as r decreases.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Work must be done against the repulsive force to bring them closer; this work is stored as electric potential energy, Eₚ = kq₁q₂/r, which increases as r decreases. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how the separation of field lines represents the strength of an electric field.
items.answer: Field strength is proportional to the number of lines passing through unit area perpendicular to them; where lines are closer together the field is stronger.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Field strength is proportional to the number of lines passing through unit area perpendicular to them; where lines are closer together the field is stronger. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "A Faraday cage gives complete protection from all electric fields and radiation."
items.answer: It shields static fields and long-wavelength radiation effectively, but not all fields, so "complete" is an overstatement.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: static fields inside a closed conductor are zero; cars protect occupants from lightning. Arguments against: holes allow radiation of wavelength smaller than the mesh to enter; magnetic fields at low frequency are not blocked; contact with the cage can still be dangerous. Supported judgement: It shields static fields and long-wavelength radiation effectively, but not all fields, so "complete" is an overstatement.

items.stem: "Static electricity is only a curiosity with no practical importance." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Electrostatics has important industrial applications and safety implications, so it is far more than a curiosity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: everyday sparks and clinging clothes seem trivial. Arguments against: electrostatic precipitators clean power-station emissions; photocopiers and laser printers use electrostatic charging; sparks can ignite fuel vapour, so earthing is vital. Supported judgement: Electrostatics has important industrial applications and safety implications, so it is far more than a curiosity. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem:
A Hall probe measures the magnetic flux density B at distances r from a long straight wire carrying 3.0 A. Theory: B = μ₀I/(2πr).

r / cm | B / μT
1.0 | 58.9
1.5 | 39.5
2.0 | 29.5
3.0 | 19.7
4.0 | 14.8
5.0 | 12.2

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the permeability of free space μ₀. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±2 %. State μ₀ with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) B in T (y) against 1/r in m⁻¹ (x); (b) gradient ≈ 5.87 × 10⁻⁷ T m; (c) 1.23 × 10⁻⁶ T m A⁻¹; (d) 1.23 × 10⁻⁶ T m A⁻¹ ± 2 × 10⁻⁸ T m A⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) B in T (y) against 1/r in m⁻¹ (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 5.87 × 10⁻⁷ T m – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) μ₀ = 2π × gradient/I = 1.23 × 10⁻⁶ T m A⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 2 % of the value = 2 × 10⁻⁸ T m A⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: "Electric potential is a more useful concept than electric field." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Neither is more useful in general; potential simplifies energy problems while field describes forces.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: potential is a scalar so contributions add simply; energy calculations use ΔV directly. Arguments against: the field gives the force and direction of motion; the two are linked by E = −ΔV/Δr, so each is used where convenient. Supported judgement: Neither is more useful in general; potential simplifies energy problems while field describes forces.
